newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam executives held in widening fraud probe.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam executives held in widening fraud probe.

text.p: Thirteen senior executives from Vietnam's debt-torn conglomerate Minh Phung have been arrested for suspected fraud, police in Ho Chi Minh City said on Thursday.
The widening net around the garments-to-property giant is the latest twist in a government offensive against corruption and economic crime.
Directors, deputy directors and the chief accountant of the garments-to-property firm Minh Phung were all detained on Wednesday by investigators with a search-and-arrest warrant.
Police declined to give further details.
The company's boss, Tang Minh Phung, was himself arrested in March -- on the same day as the chief executive of EPCO, a prominent trading company which is also based in the southern city.
Official media reports say that Minh Phung borrowed large quantities of steel and other commodities from EPCO to use as collateral for a $17.1 million loan from state-owned Vietcombank.
Bankers say some of Vietnam's banks are sitting on mountains of debt because of loans to companies which have turned bad.

Many firms are said to have used influence and connections to secure huge multiple loans from commercial banks. Those borrowings were sometimes backed by collateral which was overvalued or even committed already.
There have been various reports of the debts racked up by Minh Phung during a headlong expansion drive and heavy investment in a property market that has gone from boom to bust.

State Bank of Vietnam Governor Cao Si Kiem told the National Assembly two weeks ago that Minh Phung's debts, in local currency and dollars, came to around $26 million, of which about $5 million was overdue.
However, the official daily Saigon Giai Phong said Phung had told investigators when he was arrested that the firm's debts to banks and enterprises totalled 4.31 trillion dong ($369.6 million).

The arrest of the 13 businessmen follows several high-profile corruption and fraud trials in Ho Chi Minh City, which has become a boomtown under the government's drive to reform the economy along market lines.
Two more people were sentenced to death in January for duping the state of $12 million in cash and gold through a racket involving a fertiliser transaction.

Ten days later, four people were sent to the firing squad for their part in a multi-million-dollar embezzlement scam at Tamexco, a Ho Chi Minh City import-export firm affiliated to the country's ruling Communist Party.
Twenty-five officials are due to go on trial in coming weeks for siphoning off millions of dollars from Nam Dinh Textiles, one of the country's oldest and best-known state-owned firms.
Minh Phung, which has around 8,000 employees, was established as a garment company in 1981 and later expanded into trading, construction and real estate.
The Truoi Tre newspaper said that Phung established 20 subsidiaries to get more credit, either by borrowing directly or by importing goods with deferred letters of credit.
